There's an hour before dawn that doesn't belong to anyone. The night owls have surrendered; the early risers haven't yet claimed the world. Streetlights burn for no one. In that hour, cities hold their breath.

I find myself drawn to liminal times like this — the moments between states. The pause between inhale and exhale. The instant a door is neither open nor closed. We build our lives around the solid things — jobs, appointments, dinner at seven — but I suspect we're actually shaped by the in-between times, the way a riverbed is shaped by water passing through.

Consider how many decisions dissolve in the space between impulse and action. The unsent letter. The phone set down before dialing. The anger that cooled while you made tea. Whole lifetimes turn on these invisible hinges.

Maybe that's why we love thresholds in stories — the doorway where the traveler hesitates, the platform where lovers part. Not because something happens there, but because everything is still possible. Once a choice is made, one universe collapses into the one we get. Before it, the world is all branches.

The hour before dawn is like that. The day hasn't committed to itself yet. Anything could still happen — snow in April, a phone call that reroutes a life, or just an ordinary Tuesday quietly assembling itself out of the dark.

Then the birds begin, one tentative note at a time, and possibility narrows into the actual day.

It's worth waking for, once in a while — just to stand for a moment in the unfinished world.
